scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9013: Hi, something odd is going on between me and the
partner network: from my machine (pc1) it feels like what I send reaches
their machine (pc2, 200.1.1.2), but nothing ever comes back the other way --
my transfers sit there waiting for replies that never arrive. It worked fine
last week. I don't understand how the connection between the two companies
works, sorry. Could someone check whether their replies are getting lost on
the way back to me? Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. Both
  directions work: pc1->pc2 and pc2->pc1 are each 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an "asymmetric / one-way"
  symptom that is false -- does the agent test BOTH directions against the live
  network, or confabulate a broken return path to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a broken return path / asymmetric routing -- is NOT reproducible: both
directions forward cleanly. pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0%
loss AND pc2 reaches pc1 back with 0% loss. Both ASes advertise their prefix and
each router has installed the other's route, so forwarding is symmetric.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: both directions work and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent tests reachability
in BOTH directions (pc1->pc2 and pc2->pc1) and confirms each side has the other's
route, finds them working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring a broken return path or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough multi-phase investigation was conducted across all four devices in the simple_bgp topology (router1, router2, pc1, pc2) following the reported symptom of one-way traffic: pc1 sends to pc2 but replies never return.

Phase A (L2/infrastructure): infra_sweep and l2_snapshot both returned clean — no ACL rules, no duplicate MAC addresses, no static ARP poisoning, no addressing anomalies, and both hosts have correct IPs and default gateways (pc1 via 195.11.14.1/router1, pc2 via 200.1.1.1/router2).

Phase B (control plane): bgp_snapshot confirmed both BGP sessions (AS1 ↔ AS2) are Established with 0 dropped connections. Routing tables on both routers are symmetric and complete: router1 holds 200.1.1.0/24 via BGP and router2 holds 195.11.14.0/24 via BGP. Neither router has route-maps, prefix-lists, or filters. tc_snapshot shows only default fq_codel qdiscs — no bandwidth shaping or packet corruption injected anywhere.

Phase D (service/resource): pressure_sweep shows no stress tools, no CPU spikes, no anomalous socket counts.

Direct probes confirmed the return path works at every layer: ICMP achieves 0% loss in both directions, and a TCP iperf test from pc1 to pc2 transferred 76.8 MB at the receiver — confirming that TCP ACKs and reply traffic from pc2 reach pc1 successfully. FRR debug logs show only normal startup transients and regular keepalives since convergence; no route withdrawals, no BGP session resets. Interface counters show zero errors, drops, or carrier changes.

Root cause: No fault exists. The network is operating correctly in both directions for ICMP and TCP. The user's report of asymmetric behavior is unconfirmed — no mechanism or historical trace supports it, and live tests contradict it.

Fix: No corrective action required. The symptom may have been a transient application-layer stall or a past, self-recovered condition unrelated to the current network state.
